class Solution
  MOD = 1_000_000_007

  def num_of_arrays(n, m, k)
    # dp[i][j][cost]: number of arrays of length i, with max element j, and search cost == cost
    # max element j ranges from 1 to m
    # cost ranges from 1 to k (search_cost >= 1 always because first element sets max and cost at least 1)

    # To handle cost=0 (for ease, though not valid state), we'll use 0..k
    dp = Array.new(n + 1) { Array.new(m + 1) { Array.new(k + 1, 0) } }

    # Base case: for i=1, dp[1][j][1] = 1 for all j in 1..m
    (1..m).each do |j|
      dp[1][j][1] = 1
    end

    (2..n).each do |i|
      (1..m).each do |max_val|
        (1..k).each do |cost|
          # Case 1: current element <= max_val, so max remains max_val, no increase in cost
          # The current element can be from 1 to max_val (no new max set)
          # So we add dp[i-1][max_val][cost] * max_val (elements <= max_val)
          dp[i][max_val][cost] += (dp[i - 1][max_val][cost] * max_val) % MOD
          dp[i][max_val][cost] %= MOD

          # Case 2: current element > max_val (new max)
          # We consider all prev_max from 1..max_val-1, cost-1 (since new max found)
          # The new max element is fixed to max_val, so count dp[i-1][prev_max][cost-1] * 1
          if cost > 1
            (1...max_val).each do |prev_max|
              dp[i][max_val][cost] += dp[i - 1][prev_max][cost - 1]
              dp[i][max_val][cost] %= MOD
            end
          end
        end
      end
    end

    # sum dp[n][j][k] for j=1..m
    ans = 0
    (1..m).each do |j|
      ans += dp[n][j][k]
      ans %= MOD
    end

    ans
  end
end

**Input:** n = 5, m = 2, k = 3
**Output:** 0

**Example 3:**

**Input:** n = 9, m = 1, k = 1
**Output:** 1
**Explanation:** The only possible array is \[1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1\]

**Constraints:**

*   `1 <= m <= 100`
*   `0 <= k <= n`
